title: Good news to the poor (Isaiah 61:1–3)
hook: beauty for ashes: the passage Jesus read in Nazareth

segments.voice: Yesterday, everyone who thirsts, the market cry, and your line was without money, without price. What did you give away freely? Day four hundred seventy-two.

A small-town synagogue on the Sabbath. Everyone knows everyone. Joseph's son is back, the one people have been talking about since he started teaching around Galilee. He stands up to read. The attendant hands him a scroll of the prophet Isaiah. He unrolls it, finds the place he wants, and reads a few lines aloud. Then he rolls it back up, hands it to the attendant, and sits down. The room goes quiet. Luke's Gospel says every eye in the place was fixed on him. Today, the passage Jesus chose to read in his hometown of Nazareth.
screen: `A SABBATH IN NAZARETH.` → `JOSEPH'S SON STANDS.` → `EVERY EYE FIXED ON HIM.`

segments.voice: Isaiah sixty-one begins, in the King James Bible: "The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound." The Hebrew word behind meek also means the poor, the bowed down, the ones with no power. And anointed shares a root with the word messiah. And then the line in your carry, from verse three: "to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness." In Hebrew, beauty for ashes is a little rhyme, pe'er tachat efer. Ashes were what mourners put on their heads. Pe'er was a festive headdress, a garland. The same head that wore ashes now wears a crown. Three trades: ashes for a crown, mourning for oil of gladness, a heavy spirit for a bright cloak. Now back to Nazareth. Jesus reads from this passage, Luke tells us, and then sits down and says: "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears." Luke sets it at the start of Jesus' public work, and Christians often read it as his program: good news to the poor, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed. And look closely at where he stops. Isaiah's sentence goes on: to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God. Luke has Jesus stop after the year of the Lord's favor. He rolls up the scroll mid-sentence. Some Christian readers make much of that pause: in their reading, he came announcing favor first.
screen: `ANOINTED: GOOD TIDINGS TO THE POOR.` · `PE'ER TACHAT EFER: A CROWN FOR ASHES.` · `THIS DAY IS THIS SCRIPTURE FULFILLED.` · `HE STOPS MID-SENTENCE.` · then, large: `BEAUTY FOR ASHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who is mourning. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone wearing ashes right now, in their own way: a fresh loss, a divorce, a diagnosis, an anniversary of a death. Picture them as they are. Don't hurry them toward the garland. In the book of Job, a mourner sits in the ashes, and his friends sit down with him in silence. Then think of one small thing that could be a bit of oil of gladness for them: a meal, a note, a visit, a memory shared. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Pe'er. The festive garland Isaiah promises in place of ashes, worn by the brokenhearted and the captives: the passage Jesus read aloud in Nazareth.
Your line: beauty for ashes. Today, help one person who is mourning, in one concrete way: bring food, send the note, make the call, or just show up. Day four hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Churches often read Isaiah 61 and Luke 4 together, and Christians often describe the passage as Jesus's mission statement; it is read at ordinations and in services focused on the poor, the sick and the imprisoned.

fork.reveal: "this day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears." Luke places it at the start of Jesus' public work.

original.note: Hebrew: a garland instead of ashes. the two nouns share the same letters.

trapdoor: what you thought: beauty for ashes means things will turn out pretty.
what it means: the mourner's ashes are exchanged for a festive crown, grief for gladness, by God's anointed messenger.
what a scholar hears: pe'er and efer use the same three letters rearranged. and Luke's version includes sight to the blind, which the Hebrew of Isaiah 61 lacks, and stops before the day of vengeance.

notes: Pe'er (פאר) and efer (אפר) share the letters pe, aleph, resh in different order. Confirm the trapdoor wording.
Luke 4:18–19 follows the Septuagint ('recovering of sight to the blind') and includes a line from Isaiah 58:6; it ends at 'the acceptable year of the Lord' (Isaiah 61:2a). Confirm.
'In those synagogues, the teacher sat to teach' (cf. Luke 4:20; Matthew 5:1). Confirm.
'Anointed is the root of the word messiah' (mashach / mashiach). Confirm.
